## 289. Early warnings before seabird breeding failures, in the field (EW2)

```text
Result(s): none new about the unfolding; no record changed; no Lean. A frozen field test of thesis T6's uncoupled
       side (section 286's open item), experiments/break-warnings; reuses T6's proved half (Web.break_not_bounded)
       only as the thesis tested.
Delta: on Cury et al.'s (2011) published series, in Benguela (sardine and anchovy; gannets and penguins) and Rost
       (age-0 herring; puffins), the prey's 8-year lag-1 autocorrelation and variance before the birds' poor years
       did not exceed what the prey's level path predicts at the frozen level: V1 passed (p = 0.048), V2 passed
```

**What was asked.** Section 286 left T6's uncoupled side with one test that can fail on something the tester did not choose: real dependents whose need is measured on themselves. Cury et al. (2011) measured such a need, seabird breeding success falling below about a third of the largest forage-fish biomass. The brief asked for a literature and data check first, with a stop rule, and otherwise a test frozen before any test value was read, the matched null fixed in advance and never selected on the outcome.

**What the check found** ([significance review, seabird-warnings-check](../../BECOMING-SIGNIFICANCE-REVIEW.md#seabird-warnings-check)). The series are public: the SOM prints all 19, z-scored. Four prey series have at least 20 consecutive years. No earlier study reads forage-fish statistics before seabird failures; Burthe et al. (2016) read each series against its own turning points and found warnings rarely true. The feedback was measured by Saraux et al. (2021), whose data put the birds' share near the need at 0.3-4% at Benguela, 4-11% of Røst's age-0 herring and 26-96% for Shetland's seabird community. Shetland is therefore T6's coupled case, not its uncoupled side. Røst enters by mechanism, not by share: the index is set on 1 January, before the puffins eat that year class, and the herring's recruitment is weakly tied to its spawners. The stop rule asked for best-case power of at least 0.5 against a large effect. It was met with Røst in scope (0.66-0.72) and not for Benguela alone (0.30-0.35).

**What the test reads.** Given the stock's level path, T6 says the stock's statistics carry no information on whether the dependents fail. That conditional independence is testable; feedback is not. In the dry runs a feedback that depends on the level is matched away with it, even at a 40% share. A failure would have shown the prey's statistics knowing something about the birds' poor years that the level path does not carry: a need lying partly in the prey's variability, or a driver shared by both. The first design, a randomization over circular shifts of the dependents' residuals, rejected at up to 0.073 under null generators, about twice its level. The observed residual is orthogonal to the covariates and its shifts are not, so they are not exchangeable. It was replaced before any field value was read by the partial correlation with Pyper and Peterman's effective size, which held all five nulls at most 0.034. Both designs' rates are kept.

**What it found.** Both verdicts passed. The partial correlations were positive in both stocks for both statistics (0.23-0.43), the direction the clause names. The combined estimate is about 0.3 with an interval from no association to about 0.6. Adjusting for the level raised Røst's estimate (0.08 unadjusted, 0.26 adjusted for autocorrelation), so the stock's decline does not carry it. A 10-year window lost Røst's autocorrelation and kept Benguela's. Shetland (the coupled case) and the Farallon birds (share unmeasured) showed nothing.

**What it means for T6.** T6 survives a test it could have failed, at the frozen level, and no more. Its standing stays conjectured, with this pass recorded beside it as one of low power. The positive estimates are not evidence against T6 at the level chosen in advance, and they are not evidence for it either. They are what the next test must resolve: the same frozen design on longer, unread series, with the catch as the draw. If an association of about this size held up, T6 would need its "given the stock's own course" to carry more than the level path, either the drivers of the stock's variability or the part of the need that lies in it.

**Self-review.** Three judgments could be wrong. First, Røst's place in scope is argued on mechanism, and the stop rule passes only with it; a reader who takes "negligible share" as a share of the year class would put Røst outside, and then no test could be supported here. Second, the level covariates were chosen before the run, but other reasonable choices (the window mean in place of last year's level, a hinge at the need in place of the square) were not tried, and with 43 usable years the estimate may move with them. They were left untried so as not to pick among them after seeing results. Third, "failure" is relative here, each stock's lowest third of years, while T6's break is the dependent's activity failing. At Røst the SOM counts 18 seasons of virtually complete failure since 1975, more than a third of the years, so the relative failures there are likely seasons of that kind (not checked year by year). At Benguela the z-scores do not show where breeding stops, so the relative definition may mark poor years that are not breaks.
